message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I should ask my brother for an apology after what happened. Let me start by going through the situation step by step. First, my brother's girlfriend passed away, and her funeral was last week. We were all there, including her father, who talked a lot about God during the service. I whispered to my brother, "I wonder why God didn't save his daughter." I was just making a dark joke, I think. But my brother glared at me, which he usually does when I make those kinds of jokes. After the funeral luncheon, we went home. My brother didn't talk to me. His friends came over, and when they asked how it went, I told them I didn't care about religion being shoved down my throat. My brother got really angry, slammed the remote on the table, and called me a dumbass. He said it was her father's church and that I was twisting everything to be an oppressed victim, which is why everyone hates me. He couldn't believe I was that stupid. I told him I was going upstairs to try not to cry because I knew he hated me. He accused me of guilt-tripping him, but I really did cry. When I came back down, I asked him to apologize because what he said was hurtful. He tried to minimize how awful I felt, saying I'm just a scumbag. His friends said he took it too far, and he accused all of us of lacking empathy. Now, I'm wondering if I'm being too sensitive or if I should just let it go. I mean, he's grieving, right? But I also feel hurt and misunderstood. I don't want to come off as the victim, but his words were really harsh. I'm not sure if asking for an apology is the right move or if it's better to just give him space. I think about why I made that comment about God. Maybe I was trying to cope with the loss in my own way, but it came out as a joke. I didn't mean to offend anyone, especially not my brother during such a tough time. But I also feel like I have the right to express my feelings, even if they're different from others. When I asked for an apology, I was hoping he would acknowledge that his words were hurtful. But instead, he minimized my feelings, which made me feel even worse. I wonder if he's aware of how his actions affected me or if he's too caught up in his own grief to consider mine. I also think about the role of religion here. My brother's girlfriend's father is very religious, and that's probably why he focused so much on God during the funeral. But I don't share that belief, and it's hard for me to see how that helps in a situation like this. I guess that's why I made the comment, but I didn't realize how it would affect my brother. Now, considering whether I should ask for an apology again or not. I don't want to push him away, but I also don't want to keep feeling hurt. Maybe there's a middle ground where we can talk about it without it turning into an argument. But I'm not sure how to approach that. I also think about the advice from his friends. They said he took it too far, which makes me feel like maybe he does realize he went overboard. But he accused us all of lacking empathy, which is ironic because I felt like he was the one not understanding my perspective. In the end, I'm torn between wanting to maintain a good relationship with my brother and needing to address the hurt he caused. I don't want to hold a grudge, but I also don't want to pretend like nothing happened. I guess I need to find a way to communicate my feelings without making him defensive. Maybe I should wait a bit and give him some space to process his grief. Then, when things calm down, I can approach him calmly and express how his words affected me. I can explain that I didn't mean to offend him and that I was just trying to cope in my own way. Hopefully, he'll be able to understand and we can move forward from there. I also wonder if there's a way to bridge our different beliefs. I'm an atheist, and he seems to be more religious, especially given the situation. Maybe we can have a conversation about our beliefs and how they affect how we handle grief. That way, we can both understand each other better and avoid similar conflicts in the future. But I'm not sure if he's open to that kind of conversation, especially right now when he's still grieving. I don't want to add to his stress, but I also don't want to let this issue fester. It's a delicate balance. I think the key is to approach him with empathy and understanding, acknowledging his loss and how hard this must be for him. Then, gently express how his words made me feel and why I reacted the way I did. By showing that I care about his feelings too, maybe he'll be more open to hearing mine. In the meantime, I should focus on my own healing and not let this situation consume me. I can talk to other friends or family members about how I'm feeling to get support. It's important to take care of myself while also trying to maintain a good relationship with my brother. Overall, I think the best approach is to give him some time, then have a calm and honest conversation about our feelings. That way, we can both express ourselves and work towards understanding and healing.
